summary: Proposes a bridge that connects hosts using TCP with hosts using X.25 by relaying ISO TP0 transport connections between them. Hosts are invited to experiment with the proposal, and it reserves TCP port 146 for this purpose.

plainLanguage.summary: Two groups use different kinds of phone systems. This describes a go-between box that passes messages from one system to the other so they can talk.

subtitle: Relay ISO Transport Protocol connections between TCP/IP hosts and X.25 hosts.

tldr.problem: TCP/IP internets (like the DDN) and X.25 networks are separate worlds. Hosts on one side cannot easily communicate with hosts on the other, even if both run ISO protocols.
tldr.mechanism: A bridge host runs both TCP and X.25 connections, relaying ISO TP0 protocol packets between them. TCP/IP hosts register with the bridge to reach X.25 addresses; X.25 hosts call the bridge's registered addresses. Once connected, packets flow transparently.
tldr.outcome: TCP/IP sites with sparse X.25 links can give all users transparent access to X.25 hosts running ISO protocols, avoiding the need for separate logins.

today: RFC 1086 is Unknown status and has not been obsoleted. The TP0 bridge was an experimental approach to DDN/ISO interoperability. Modern networking has largely moved toward TCP/IP as the dominant protocol suite, reducing the need for X.25 bridges. However, the concept of transparent protocol relaying at defined layers remains relevant for network interoperability.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The ISO-TP0 bridge connects hosts using TCP/IP with hosts using X.25 networks by relaying protocol packets at the ISO Transport Protocol layer. This is useful when a site has both a TCP/IP local area network and a connection to an X.25 public network or private X.25 cloud, and needs to give TCP/IP users access to ISO services on X.25.

The bridge is not a general solution to DDN/ISO interoperability, but rather applies when both sides of the connection run ISO Transport Protocol version 0 (TP0). RFC 1006 defined how to run TP0 over TCP/IP; the bridge combines this with the standard method of running TP0 over X.25, applying both as appropriate. The bridge operates by relaying packets transparently once a connection is established, with a simple registration protocol for the connection setup phase.

Two scenarios justify the bridge. First, a TCP/IP host can communicate with X.25 hosts if both run ISO protocols, provided a bridge host offers X.25 address space. Second, a site with a LAN and sparse X.25 connectivity can give all LAN users access to X.25-based ISO hosts without requiring them to log into the X.25 cloud separately.
sections.plainLanguage: A bridge box sits between a TCP/IP network and an X.25 network. It lets computers on one side call computers on the other, passing protocol messages between them.

sections.title: Protocol Concepts
sections.content:
The ISO Transport Service provides reliable packet-stream communication to applications. The ISO Transport Protocol (TP) implements this service in five classes, selected based on the underlying network's capabilities. TP0 is the simplest class, used when the network is connection-oriented and error-detecting—for example, X.25 or TCP.

X.25 is a connection-oriented, error-detecting network service standardized by CCITT (now ITU) as a wide-area network offering. It is popular in Europe and communities with strong PTT infrastructure.

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is the transport layer of the DoD Internet Protocol Suite, running over IP. Although TCP is technically an end-to-end transport protocol rather than a network protocol, RFC 1006 showed that the ISO transport service can be layered on top of TCP/IP, treating the pair as a network service. This flexibility of layering enables the bridge concept: both TCP/IP and X.25 can appear as suitable network services to TP0, so TP0 packets can be relayed between them.
sections.plainLanguage: Both X.25 and TCP are reliable connection services. TP0 is a simple protocol that assumes the connection below it is reliable, so it works the same way on both.

sections.title: Bridge Operation and Connection Establishment
sections.content:
Once a TP0 connection is established between a TCP host and an X.25 host (or both via the bridge), the bridge simply relays TP0 packets in both directions. During data transfer, it reads transport protocol data units (TPDUs) from one connection and writes them to the other. When either side disconnects, the bridge disconnects the other side; if both disconnect simultaneously, no action is needed.

Connection establishment is more complex. A TCP/IP host initiates connection by establishing a TCP connection to the bridge on port 146. It then sends a one-octet function code indicating which of two operations to perform: connect to a remote X.25 address, or listen for incoming X.25 connections.

Function 1 (outgoing call): The TCP host sends an X.25 address. The bridge attempts to call that address. If successful, TP0 data transfer begins. If the call fails, the bridge closes the TCP connection.

Function 2 (listening): The TCP host sends an X.25 subaddress (part of the bridge's address space) and a TCP/IP address and port to receive incoming calls. The bridge listens on that X.25 address. When an incoming call arrives, the bridge establishes a TCP connection to the registered TCP/IP address. If successful, data transfer begins; if not, the incoming call is refused. The bridge uses the TCP/IP connection as a heartbeat; if it closes, the bridge stops listening on that X.25 address.
sections.plainLanguage: To call an X.25 computer from TCP/IP, you connect to the bridge and tell it what X.25 address to call. To let X.25 computers call you, you register your TCP/IP address and an X.25 mailbox number with the bridge.

sections.title: Address Format Specifications
sections.content:
The protocol defines standard octet encodings for X.25 and TCP/IP addresses, allowing addresses to be transmitted uniformly.

X.25 addresses use a fixed-length 68-octet format with ten fields: address type (2 octets, value 3), X.121 address (16 ASCII octets, the actual X.25 address like a phone number), X.121 length (1 octet indicating how many of the 16 are meaningful), Protocol ID (4 octets), Protocol ID length (1 octet), User Data (16 octets), User Data length (1 octet), X.25 Facilities (6 octets), and Facilities length (1 octet). These length fields allow variable-length content packed into fixed space.

TCP/IP addresses use a fixed-length 16-octet format with four fields: address type (2 octets, value 2), TCP port (2 octets in network order), IP address (4 octets in network order), and reserved padding (16 octets of zeros).

The memo notes these formats are somewhat ad-hoc and Unix-specific. They may change as experience is gained with the TP0 bridge.
sections.plainLanguage: Both X.25 and TCP/IP addresses are packed into standard fixed-length formats so the bridge can parse them reliably. Each format specifies type, the actual address, and optional extra data.

sections.title: Authentication and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC explicitly ignores authentication and authorization, treating these as local policy matters. A bridge operator must implement access control to prevent unauthorized use of the bridge's X.25 address space.

Without restrictions, any TCP/IP host can lay claim to part of the bridge's X.25 address space by registering listening addresses (Function 2). X.25 address space is limited and cannot support many foreign hosts registering addresses. Operators should implement local authentication to ensure only authorized hosts register X.25 listening addresses.

Additionally, passwords and credentials for remote hosts must be stored securely on the bridge host. The RFC notes that the security of these credentials depends on the file system security of the BFTP/bridge control host.
sections.plainLanguage: The bridge needs to know who it trusts. An operator should restrict which computers can register X.25 mailboxes, and keep stored passwords secure.
